inputs.need:
I am a public health physician at a regional health unit that runs the heat-health action plan for about 700,000 people. When the forecast reaches our activation threshold, two days above 31 degrees with night-time lows above 20, we issue public alerts, open cooling centres, call about 4,000 registered vulnerable residents and ask hospitals to prepare. Last summer the plan was activated on 7 days, but emergency departments reported heat-related visits on at least 15 other days, and our board is asking whether we should lower the threshold and what that would cost.

I would like to write a narrative review for the board before the 2027 heat season: what the published evidence says about whether activating a heat plan reduces emergency department visits and ambulance calls, what happens when the threshold is lowered, who benefits and who does not, and what activation costs. I do not have the time or data for a formal pooled analysis, and much of the relevant literature is time-series studies and reports from other health units. The board members are not clinicians, so the review has to be clear about how certain each finding is.

I need help framing the questions, deciding which kinds of studies and reports to include, how to present effects on emergency visits alongside what activation costs without pretending we can calculate value for money, and how to show equity effects, especially for older people living alone and low-income neighbourhoods. The review has to be done by me and an epidemiology resident over the winter.

records.title: Heat-health alert activation and emergency department visits for heat-related illness: a time-series study in four cities
records.authors: Moreau-Adebayo L, Kristiansen-Oduro P, Castillo-Webb T
records.abstract: We analysed daily emergency department visits in four cities over eight summers, comparing days when a heat-health alert was active with non-alert days of similar temperature. Heat-related emergency department visits were lower on alert days (rate ratio 0.83, 95 percent CI 0.74 to 0.93). All-cause emergency department visits did not change. The association was weaker in the city with the fewest cooling centres. Because alerts are issued on the hottest days, residual confounding by temperature is possible despite matching, and the study could not say which parts of the plan mattered.

records.title: What does it cost to activate a heat-health action plan? A regional costing study
records.abstract: We costed three summers of heat-health action plan activations in one region, including cooling centre staffing, outreach calls, communications and hospital preparedness. The mean cost per activation day was 42,000, of which cooling centres accounted for more than half. Costs rose with the number of consecutive activation days because staff overtime increased. The study did not estimate health effects, so a cost per emergency visit avoided could not be calculated. Costs borne by hospitals and by residents were not included.

records.title: Lowering the activation threshold of a heat alert system: changes in activation days and heat-related morbidity
records.authors: Petrakis-Oyelowo J, Svensson-Achebe N, Rao-Fitzgerald D
records.abstract: A health unit lowered the temperature threshold for activating its heat alert system by 2 degrees. Activation days rose from a mean of 6 to 14 per summer. On the newly covered days, heat-related emergency department visits were 9 percent below the number expected from the previous threshold's pattern (95 percent CI -3 to 20 percent). Staff reported alert fatigue in the public and among partner agencies after long runs of activation. The evaluation covered two summers and had no comparison region.

records.title: Heat-health warning systems and health outcomes: a systematic review
records.abstract: We included 22 studies of heat-health warning systems, none of them randomised. Most were time-series or before-after analyses of mortality; 9 of 14 mortality studies reported fewer deaths during warnings than expected. Only 5 studies examined emergency department visits or ambulance calls, with mixed results. Studies rarely separated the effects of different plan components and rarely reported effects by age, income or living alone. The review concludes that warning systems probably reduce heat mortality but that effects on emergency care use are uncertain.

records.title: How older adults respond to heat alerts: an interview study
records.abstract: We interviewed 30 adults aged 70 and over living alone during a summer with repeated heat alerts. Many did not consider themselves at risk and did not change their routines in response to public alerts. Outreach telephone calls from someone they recognised were more likely to lead to action, such as drinking more or visiting a cooler place. Cooling centres were seen as hard to reach without a car. Several participants were unaware that an alert was in effect because they did not follow local news.

records.title: Evaluation of a municipal cooling centre programme during heat alerts
records.abstract: We evaluated attendance at 12 cooling centres opened during heat alerts over two summers. Cooling centres were used by an estimated 3 percent of residents in the targeted vulnerable groups. Most visitors were younger adults who lived nearby; older residents cited transport and uncertainty about opening hours as barriers. A pilot of free transport to two centres doubled visits by residents aged over 70 at those sites. Opening hours were extended in the second summer without a clear change in attendance. The evaluation did not measure health outcomes.

records.title: Heat-related emergency department visits by neighbourhood income during heat alerts
records.authors: Nwosu-Lindqvist B, Garcia-Holt E, Mensah-Kowalczyk T
records.abstract: We linked heat-related emergency department visits to neighbourhood income in one metropolitan region over six summers. On alert days, visit rates were 2.4 times higher in the lowest income fifth than in the highest. The reduction in visits associated with alerts was smaller in the lowest income fifth than in the highest. Neighbourhoods with less tree cover and more rented housing had the highest rates. The authors recommend targeting outreach and cooling resources to low-income neighbourhoods rather than relying on public alerts alone.

response.synthesis: Seven retrieved records, appraised at abstract level. Time-series evidence associates heat alerts with fewer heat-related emergency visits, but a review of 22 non-randomised studies found only 5 on emergency care, with mixed results. Lowering the threshold more than doubled activation days in one unit, with an uncertain effect on visits whose interval includes none. A regional costing gives the cost of an activation day but no health effect, so value for money cannot be computed. Older people living alone and low-income neighbourhoods benefit least from public alerts; outreach calls and transport to cooling centres help.
response.gradeRationale: Observational time-series and before-after evidence with possible confounding by temperature; the threshold evidence is imprecise; costs are known but not linked to effects.

response.reading: Activation is associated with fewer heat-related emergency visits, but which components help, and whether a lower threshold adds benefit, is uncertain. Outreach and transport look more promising than alerts alone.
